newsitem.title: UK: Sterling tumbles on technicals, rates nerves.
newsitem.headline: Sterling tumbles on technicals, rates nerves.

text.p: Sterling extended its slide at the European midsession on Wednesday, dragged down by a move below key technical levels and nervousness ahead of the outcome of the Bank of England's monetary policy committee meeting.
"It's reminiscent of last week," said David Coleman, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy. "Selling began with cable on stops and brought down sterling/mark."

The pound lost more than four pfennigs and over three cents from session highs. It was at $1.5962/72 - its lowest in nearly five-months - from $1.6262/72 in late European trading on Tuesday. Sterling/mark was at 3.0141/51 against 3.0545/56.
Many traders still bet on a 25 basis points rise in interest rates to 7.00 percent but doubts that the MPC will act for the fourth month in a row have crept into the market.

Analysts cited signs that sterling's strength is not only hurting exporters but also beginning to damage competitiveness of UK services providers. This was highlighted in a survey from the Chartered Institute of Purchasing and Supply released on Tuesday.
Coleman said he still expected a 25 basis points rise. "This may increasingly be seen as a near-term plateau ... Fears by some of an eight percent rate would prove misplaced."
"We may be seeing a first glimmer of light. They (interest rates) could sit for a couple of months," said Coleman.
A Reuter poll said 16 out of 23 economists surveyed expected rates to rise from their current level of 6.75 percent to 7.0 percent - the fourth-quarter point increase since May.

The sterling downmove was led by an initial bout of profit-taking on cable, sparked by U.S. and Asian names. It pushed cable through stops around key support of $1.62 - dragging sterling/mark in its wake.
"Once sterling went throught he $1.62 area it hit stops...People are perhaps hedging their bets for no-change in the BoE's monetary policy committee," said Peter Wood, trader at Bank of Boston.
"People are getting panicky and jumping on the bandwagon while it is moving," said Wood.
Traders said there is mounting concern as the general strength of sterling, which scaled to 3.0878 marks and its highest since August 1989 in late July, chokes off exports and threatens unemployment.
Sterling's trade-weighed index stood at 104.2 compared to its close of 105.7 on Tuesday.
"The market is getting very nervous and is starting to take profits (at these levels)," said Lee Ferridge, currency strategist at Commerzbank.
